description.en: The 45-degree side bend positions yourself sideways on a 45-degree back extension bench and performs lateral flexion — bending sideways and returning upright. It provides a greater range and load on the obliques than standing side bends.

en: Position yourself sideways on a 45-degree back extension bench. Your hip is on the pad, feet locked.
Your torso hangs freely to the side.
Cross your arms over your chest or place hands behind your head.
Lower your torso sideways toward the floor (lateral flexion).
Contract your obliques to lift your torso back to horizontal or slightly above.
Complete reps, then switch sides.
Hold a plate for added resistance when bodyweight becomes easy.
Aim for 12 to 15 reps per side.
Greater oblique range and load than standing side bends
Gravity provides constant resistance
Easy to add weight with a plate
Builds oblique strength through full range
Develops lateral core power
Simple setup

description.en: The assisted triceps dip is a regression of the standard dip performed on an assisted dip machine or with a resistance band looped around the bars. The assistance reduces your effective body weight, allowing you to build the pressing strength needed for full bodyweight dips. It trains the same muscles — triceps, chest, and shoulders — with adjustable difficulty.

en: Set up on an assisted dip machine. Select the appropriate counterweight — more weight means more assistance.
Kneel or stand on the assistance platform. Grip the parallel bars with arms locked out, supporting your weight.
Keep your torso upright for tricep emphasis (or lean forward for more chest involvement).
Tuck your elbows close to your sides. Brace your core.
Lower your body by bending at the elbows. Descend until your upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor.
Press back up by extending at the elbows. Drive your hands into the bars.
Lock out at the top. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Reduce the assistance weight over time as you get stronger, progressing toward bodyweight dips.
Effective progression toward bodyweight dips
Adjustable difficulty via counterweight selection
Trains the triceps, chest, and shoulders with reduced load
Allows higher rep volume than bodyweight dips for beginners
Builds the pressing strength needed for advanced calisthenics
Easy to track progress by reducing assistance over time

description.en: The band 45 degrees biceps curl is performed with the arms held out at roughly 45 degrees from the body during the curl. The angled position places more emphasis on the long head of the biceps. The band provides increasing tension at the top of the curl, where biceps activation is highest.

en: Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet shoulder-width apart.
Hold a handle in each hand with palms facing forward.
Bring your arms out to about 45 degrees from your body.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
Curl the handles up toward your shoulders.
Maintain the 45-degree arm angle throughout.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top.
Lower the handles slowly back to the start.
Targets the biceps long head
Emphasizes the outer arm
Increasing tension at the top
Builds biceps peak
Joint-friendly variation
Useful for arm shape and detail

description.en: The band bent over row is a horizontal pulling exercise performed by standing on a resistance band and rowing both ends up to your torso while hinged at the hips. It builds the lats, mid-traps, and rear delts with increasing tension at the peak contraction. It is one of the best at-home back exercises.

en: Stand on the center of a resistance band with feet hip-width apart.
Grip both ends of the band (or the band itself). Hinge forward at the hips to roughly 45 degrees.
Let the band hang at arm’s length. Set your back flat and brace your core.
Row both hands up toward your lower ribs by driving your elbows back.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top. Hold one second.
Lower under control. Maintain the hip-hinge position throughout.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Use a thicker band or choke up on the band for more resistance.
Builds the back with increasing tension at peak contraction
Highly portable — needs only one band
Effective at-home back exercise
Trains the lats, mid-traps, and rear delts
Easy to scale by changing band thickness
Joint-friendly with lower absolute loads

description.en: The band lying leg raise loops a resistance band around the feet (anchored behind your head or on a low post) and performs a lying leg raise against band tension. The band overloads the lower abs and hip flexors. It is an upgrade over standard leg raises for abs hypertrophy.

en: Lie on your back with arms by your sides or holding an anchor overhead.
Loop a resistance band around your feet, anchored behind your head.
Keep your legs together with a slight bend in the knees.
Brace your core and press your lower back into the floor.
Lift both legs up toward the ceiling.
Continue until your hips start to lift off the floor.
Squeeze your abs hard at the top.
Lower the legs slowly back to just above the floor.
Loaded lower ab work
Constant band tension
Builds lower abdominal strength
Stronger than bodyweight version
Easy to set up at home

description.en: The band one arm standing wide grip low row is a unilateral back exercise. Pulling the band with the elbow flared wide emphasizes the upper back, rhomboids, and rear deltoids over the lats.

en: Anchor a resistance band at low height.
Stand facing the anchor and hold the band in one hand.
Step back to create tension and stand tall with feet shoulder width.
Hinge slightly forward at the hips with a flat back.
Brace the core and pull the band up toward your shoulder.
Drive the elbow back and out wide rather than along the side.
Squeeze the upper back and rear delt at the top.
Lower the band slowly back to full arm extension and complete all reps then switch.
Hits the upper back and rear delts through the wide elbow path.
Constant band tension keeps the back loaded.
Single arm work corrects imbalances.
Joint friendly with band resistance.
Travel friendly with portable band.
Adds variety to standard rowing patterns.

description.en: The band straight-leg deadlift is a hip hinge exercise where you stand on a resistance band and hinge forward with straight legs, then stand up against the band tension. It targets the hamstrings and glutes with constant band resistance, mimicking a barbell stiff-leg deadlift.

en: Stand on the center of a resistance band with feet hip-width apart.
Hold both ends of the band at your sides or in front of your thighs.
Keep your legs straight (just a slight knee bend). Back flat.
Hinge at the hips, pushing your butt back and lowering your torso toward the floor.
Lower until you feel a deep stretch in your hamstrings.
Drive your hips forward to stand up against the band tension.
Squeeze your glutes at the top.
Use a thicker band for more resistance. Aim for 10 to 15 reps.
Builds hamstring and glute strength at home
Constant band tension throughout
Teaches the hip hinge pattern
Highly portable
Easy to scale
Useful when no barbell is available

description.en: The barbell clean high pull is an Olympic weightlifting accessory exercise where you perform the pull portion of a clean explosively without catching the bar. The bar travels up to roughly chest or chin height through hip extension and an explosive shrug. It builds the second pull of the clean and develops massive trap and posterior chain power.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart, barbell on the floor in front of you.
Squat down and grip the bar with hands just outside your knees, overhand grip.
Set your back flat. Brace your core. Lift your chest.
Begin the lift like a deadlift — drive through your feet and stand up.
As the bar passes your knees, accelerate by extending your hips and knees explosively.
At the top of the hip extension, shrug your shoulders hard and pull the bar up with high elbows.
Pull the bar to roughly chest or chin height. Do NOT catch — let the bar drop back to the floor.
Reset and repeat. Use moderate weight focused on speed and explosiveness.
Builds the explosive second pull of the clean
Develops massive trap and back power
Useful Olympic lifting accessory
Builds posterior chain explosiveness
Trains rate of force development
Less technical than full cleans

description.en: The barbell front rack split squat combines the demands of a front-loaded squat with single-leg work. Holding the bar across the front shoulders forces an upright torso while you split squat, building quads, glutes, and core stability all at once. The unilateral pattern reveals and corrects strength imbalances.

en: Position a barbell across your front shoulders in a clean rack grip with elbows high.
Step forward with your right leg into a split stance.
Stand tall with most of your weight on the front leg and the back heel raised.
Brace your core and keep your elbows pointed forward.
Lower into a split squat by bending the front knee until the back knee approaches the floor.
Maintain an upright torso throughout.
Drive through the front foot to stand back to the starting position.
Complete reps on one leg before switching sides.
Trains single-leg strength with the front rack position
Forces upright torso and strong core engagement
Builds quads and glutes unilaterally
Corrects left-right strength imbalances
Strong carryover to Olympic lifting
Less spinal load than back-loaded split squats

description.en: The barbell low split squat takes the standard split squat to its deepest range, with the back knee touching the floor at the bottom of each rep. The extreme depth builds strength through the full range of motion and develops hip and ankle mobility under load.

en: Position a barbell across your upper back in a back squat grip.
Step forward with your right leg into a split stance.
Set your back foot in a comfortable position with the heel raised.
Brace your core and lift your chest.
Lower into a split squat by bending both knees deeply.
Continue lowering until your back knee touches the floor lightly.
Drive through both legs to stand back up to the starting position.
Complete reps on one leg before switching to the other.
Builds strength through the full range of motion
Develops hip and ankle mobility under load
Trains both legs unilaterally
Corrects strength imbalances
Adductor and hip flexor stretch under load
Strong glute and quad development

description.en: The barbell rear lunge (reverse lunge) is a lunge variation where you step backward into a lunge with a barbell across your upper back. Stepping backward is generally easier on the knees than stepping forward and keeps more constant tension on the front leg throughout the movement.

en: Set a barbell at upper-back height in a power rack. Step under and place it across your upper traps.
Unrack the bar and step back. Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Step your right foot back two to three feet behind you.
Lower your right knee toward the floor by bending both knees.
Descend until your right knee is just above the floor.
Drive through your front (left) foot to push back to standing.
Alternate legs or complete all reps on one side before switching.
Keep your torso upright throughout.
Easier on the knees than forward lunges
Keeps tension on the front leg
Builds quad and glute strength unilaterally
Easy to load progressively with barbell
Exposes left-right imbalances
Useful for leg hypertrophy

description.en: The barbell reverse grip floor press combines an underhand (supinated) grip with the floor press position. The reverse grip targets the upper chest, the floor stops the descent for shoulder safety, and the partial range allows heavier loading. It is a strong choice for upper chest specialization.

en: Lie on the floor with a barbell on low rack pins.
Plant your feet flat on the floor with knees bent.
Grip the bar with palms facing you (underhand grip), shoulder-width apart.
Use a spotter to safely hand off the bar.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Hold the bar over your upper chest with arms extended.
Lower the bar with control until your elbows touch the floor.
Press the bar back up by squeezing the chest. Lock out at the top.
Targets upper chest with reverse grip
Floor protects the shoulders
Reduces front delt involvement
Heavy tricep engagement
Useful for chest specialization
Practical for home training

description.en: The barbell standing wide grip curl is performed with hands wider than shoulder-width on the barbell. The wide grip shifts emphasis to the short head of the biceps, building inner arm thickness. It is a strong complement to close grip curls for full bicep development.

en: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart.
Hold a barbell with an underhand grip, hands wider than shoulder-width.
Pin your elbows against your sides.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Curl the bar up by bending only at the elbows.
Continue until the bar reaches shoulder height.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top.
Lower the bar back down with control to full extension.
Targets short head of biceps
Builds inner arm thickness
Different stimulus than close grip curls
Pairs well with close grip for full development
Useful for breaking through curl plateaus
Strong forearm engagement

description.en: The barbell sumo deadlift from deficit is performed standing on a small platform or weight plates, raising your feet so the bar starts below your normal floor position. The extended range forces a deeper hinge and more knee flexion in the sumo stance, building bottom-end strength right where most lifters are weakest off the floor.

en: Stand on a small platform or 25 to 45 pound weight plates, around 1 to 4 inches tall.
Set up over the loaded barbell with a wide sumo stance.
Bend at the hips and knees to grip the bar with hands inside your legs.
Pull the slack out and engage your lats.
Brace your core hard.
Drive your knees out and push the floor away to start the lift.
Stand up tall with the bar, locking out hips and knees.
Lower the bar with control back to the platform.
Extended range builds bottom-end strength
Forces deeper hinge and stronger leg drive
Develops explosive drive off the floor in sumo
Improves competition sumo starting position
Tougher than standard sumo deadlifts at the same weight
Builds adductor and quad strength

description.en: The bench dip on the floor is a simplified dip variation with hands placed on the floor behind you rather than on a bench. The limited range makes it the easiest dip regression, suitable for beginners building tricep strength.

en: Sit on the floor. Place hands behind you, fingers pointing forward.
Bend knees with feet flat on the floor.
Lift your hips off the floor by pressing through your hands.
Bend your elbows to lower your body.
Press back up to lockout.
Keep your back close to your hands.
Extend legs for more difficulty.
Aim for 12 to 20 reps.
Easiest dip regression
No bench needed
Builds basic tricep strength
Accessible for beginners
Floor limits range for safety
Progresses to bench and bar dips

description.en: The bodyweight front plank to downward dog is a flowing mobility drill that alternates between two yoga style positions. It stretches the back of the legs, opens the shoulders, and strengthens the core.

en: Start in a high plank with hands under shoulders and body straight.
Brace the core and keep the head in line with the spine.
Push the hips up and back into a downward dog position.
Press the chest toward the thighs and aim heels toward the floor.
Spread the fingers wide and press through the full hand.
Hold the downward dog position for a breath.
Shift forward back into the plank with hips lowered to neutral.
Continue flowing between the two positions for the full set.
Stretches the hamstrings and calves through the dog position.
Opens the shoulders and lats with the inverted V shape.
Strengthens the core and shoulders in the plank.
Improves shoulder mobility and overhead control.
Decompresses the spine through the hip hinge.
No equipment needed and travel friendly.

description.en: The boxing block is a fundamental defensive movement in boxing where you lift your forearm and rotate it to deflect an incoming punch. As a shadowbox drill or partner exercise, it builds shoulder endurance, defensive reflexes, and cardiovascular conditioning while training the muscles used to absorb impact.

en: Stand in an orthodox boxing stance — left foot forward, right foot back, hands up at chin level.
Keep your elbows in at your sides. Forearms vertical.
To block on the right side: lift your right forearm up, palm forward, deflecting an incoming punch with your forearm or open palm.
To block on the left side: lift your left forearm in the same way.
Practice quick, snappy blocking motions in shadowbox patterns.
Combine blocks with returning punches for combination drills.
Stay light on your feet. Keep your guard up.
Practice for 30 to 60 second rounds.
Builds shoulder endurance
Develops defensive reflexes
Excellent cardiovascular conditioning
Trains coordination and reaction time
No equipment needed for shadowwork
Foundational boxing skill

description.en: The butt bridge is the standard glute bridge — lying on your back and thrusting your hips upward. It is the most fundamental glute exercise and a cornerstone of lower-body training and rehabilitation.

en: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat, hip-width apart.
Arms at sides, palms down.
Drive through your heels to lift your hips.
Squeeze your glutes hard at the top.
Body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders.
Lower under control.
Aim for 15 to 20 reps.
The most fundamental glute exercise.
Most fundamental glute exercise
Cornerstone of lower-body training
No equipment needed
Supports lower back health
Builds glute activation awareness
Progressive to all hip thrust variations

description.en: The cable bent over neutral grip kickback with rope attachment hammers the triceps. The rope splits at the end so each hand pulls separately while the cable provides steady tension throughout.

en: Set a cable pulley to the lowest setting and attach a rope.
Stand facing the cable holding one rope end in each hand.
Hinge at the hips so the torso is angled forward.
Tuck the elbows close to the sides at ninety degrees.
Brace the core and keep the upper arms still.
Extend the elbows back by squeezing the triceps.
Stop at full extension with the rope ends pulled apart.
Lower with control and repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Isolates the triceps long head.
Cable provides constant tension throughout.
Rope allows the hands to separate at lockout.
Carryover to pressing strength.
Easy to scale by adjusting cable weight.
Develops triceps lockout strength.

description.en: The cable bent over reverse grip row is performed bent forward at the hips, rowing a cable bar with a supinated (underhand) grip. The reverse grip biases the lower lats and adds biceps involvement. The constant cable tension builds back thickness without lower back swing.

en: Set a cable to a low position with a straight bar attached.
Stand facing the cable and grab the bar with an underhand grip.
Step back and hinge forward at the hips with a flat back.
Keep a slight bend in your knees.
Brace your core and let your arms hang straight down toward the cable.
Pull the bar back toward your lower abdomen.
Keep your elbows tucked close to your sides.
Squeeze the lats and lower back, then return slowly.
Targets the lower lats
Adds biceps involvement
Constant cable tension
Builds back thickness
Strong reverse grip variation
Useful for hypertrophy

description.en: The cable cross over lateral pulldown uses two cable stations with the cables crossed in front of your body. Each hand grips the opposite-side cable, creating crossing tension during the pulldown. The crossover pattern hits each lat individually and adds a unique pulling angle compared to standard pulldowns.

en: Stand between two high cable pulleys with single handles attached.
Reach across with your right hand to grip the left cable handle.
Reach across with your left hand to grip the right cable handle.
Step back to create tension and stand tall.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders down.
Pull both handles down and out to your sides simultaneously.
Squeeze your lats hard at the bottom of the pull.
Slowly extend your arms back overhead to the starting position.
Crossing tension hits each lat individually
Different angle than standard pulldown
Strong lat engagement
Builds back width
Constant cable tension through the pull
Useful for breaking through lat plateaus

description.en: The cable floor seated wide grip row is performed seated on the floor in front of a low cable pulley. A wide-grip bar is rowed back to the chest with the elbows flared. The floor seat eliminates the bench and forces strict pulling form. It builds upper back detail and is great for beginners.

en: Sit on the floor in front of a low cable pulley.
Attach a long bar or wide-grip handle to the cable.
Plant your feet flat on the floor with knees bent.
Grab the bar with a wide overhand grip and arms extended.
Brace your core and sit upright.
Pull the bar back toward your upper chest.
Lead with the elbows out to the sides at shoulder height.
Squeeze the upper back, then return slowly to the start.
Builds upper back detail
Targets rhomboids and rear delts
No bench required
Strict floor seated form
Strong upper back builder
Beginner-friendly variation

description.en: The clock push-up performs push-ups while walking the hands around in a circle (like clock positions) between reps. Each rep is at a slightly different hand angle, providing varied chest and shoulder loading throughout the set.

en: Start in a push-up position.
Perform one push-up.
Walk your hands to a new position — rotating clockwise around an imaginary clock face.
Perform another push-up at the new angle.
Continue walking hands and doing push-ups around the full circle.
Each position loads the chest and shoulders differently.
Reverse direction on the next set.
Aim for 8 to 12 positions around the clock.
Varied loading angles in one set
Targets the chest from multiple positions
No equipment needed
Engaging and creative variation
Builds adaptable pressing strength
Develops body awareness

description.en: The dumbbell devil's press is a brutal CrossFit conditioning exercise where you perform a burpee with two dumbbells in your hands, then snatch them both overhead in one motion. It is functionally a burpee combined with a double dumbbell snatch and ranks among the most demanding conditioning exercises.

en: Stand with two dumbbells on the floor in front of your feet, slightly wider than shoulder width.
Hinge down and grip both dumbbells.
Jump or step both feet back into a high plank position with hands on the dumbbells.
Lower into a push-up. Press back up.
Jump or step your feet forward to land just behind the dumbbells.
From the hinge position, explosively swing both dumbbells up and overhead in one motion (a snatch).
Catch both dumbbells locked out overhead, standing tall.
Lower the dumbbells back to the floor and repeat.
Brutal full-body conditioning
Combines push, hinge, and overhead press in one rep
CrossFit benchmark exercise
Trains explosive hip drive and overhead stability
Burns calories at an elite rate
Time-efficient conditioning

description.en: The dumbbell incline alternate press performs the incline dumbbell press one arm at a time. While one dumbbell stays at chest level, the other presses up to lockout. The alternating pattern adds core anti-rotation work and lengthens time under tension on each side of the chest.

en: Set a bench to a 30 to 45 degree incline.
Lie back with a dumbbell in each hand at chest level, palms facing forward.
Plant your feet and pull your shoulder blades back.
Brace your core hard.
Press the right dumbbell up to lockout while keeping the left dumbbell at chest level.
Lower the right dumbbell back to chest level with control.
Press the left dumbbell up to lockout while the right stays still.
Alternate sides for the full set.
Adds core anti-rotation challenge
Increases time under tension on each side
Builds upper chest strength unilaterally
Corrects left-right imbalances
Strong stability demand
Useful for breaking through pressing plateaus

description.en: The dumbbell seated alternate press performs the seated dumbbell shoulder press one arm at a time. While one dumbbell stays at the shoulder, the working arm presses to lockout. The alternating pattern increases time under tension on each side and adds anti-lateral-flexion core demand.

en: Sit on a bench with back support, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height.
Position the dumbbells with palms facing forward.
Plant your feet flat and brace your core.
Press the right dumbbell straight up overhead while keeping the left at shoulder level.
Lock out the right arm at the top.
Lower the right dumbbell back to shoulder level with control.
Press the left dumbbell up to lockout while the right stays still.
Alternate sides for the full set.
Increases time under tension on each side
Builds shoulder strength unilaterally
Adds anti-lateral-flexion core challenge
Corrects left-right imbalances
Strong stability demand
Useful for breaking through shoulder plateaus

description.en: The dumbbell standing windmill is performed standing with a dumbbell pressed overhead. Bending at the hips and reaching the opposite hand to the floor while keeping the dumbbell overhead trains hip mobility, oblique strength, and shoulder stability simultaneously. It is a classic full-body mobility and strength drill.

en: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width, toes turned out at about 45 degrees.
Press a dumbbell overhead with your right arm fully extended.
Keep your eyes on the dumbbell throughout the movement.
Place your left hand on your inner thigh.
Push your hips back to your right side as you bend forward and to the left.
Slide your left hand down your inner thigh toward the floor.
Keep the dumbbell directly overhead with arm vertical.
Reverse the motion to stand back to the starting position. Complete reps, then switch sides.
Builds hip mobility and oblique strength
Trains shoulder stability under load
Stretches hamstrings and adductors
Strong functional movement pattern
Develops total body coordination
Useful as a warm-up or accessory

description.en: The dumbbell straight leg russian twist is a tougher version of the classic Russian twist with the legs held out straight in a V position. The straight legs increase the demand on the hip flexors and core while the dumbbell adds resistance for oblique strength.

en: Sit on the floor and lean back slightly to form a V with the body.
Extend your legs straight out and lift them off the floor.
Hold a dumbbell with both hands at chest level.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
Twist the torso to bring the dumbbell to one side.
Tap the dumbbell to the floor next to your hip.
Twist back through center to the other side.
Keep legs straight and lifted throughout the set.
Brutal oblique builder
Loaded core work
Trains hip flexor strength
Improves balance
Tough V-sit position
Strong rotational power

description.en: The exercise ball lower back prone stretch is a passive lower back release. Draping the body face down over a stability ball lets the lumbar spine round forward and decompress under bodyweight.

en: Kneel in front of a stability ball.
Lower the body forward over the ball.
Allow the abdomen and chest to drape over the top.
Set the arms relaxed at the sides or in front.
Set the feet wide on the floor for support.
Allow the spine to round and the back to relax.
Breathe slowly and deeply.
Hold for the desired duration.
Decompresses the lower back.
Stretches the spine.
Useful after heavy lifting.
Joint friendly release.
Calms the nervous system.

description.en: Fish Pose (Matsyasana) is a supine yoga backbend where you lie on your back and arch your upper back off the floor, resting the crown of your head lightly on the mat. It opens the chest, throat, and front of the body while stretching the neck. It is often used as a counter pose to shoulder stand.

en: Lie flat on your back with legs extended and feet together. Arms at your sides.
Place your hands palms-down underneath your hips. Slide your forearms and elbows under your body.
Press your forearms and elbows into the floor.
Lift your chest and arch your upper back off the floor.
Tilt your head back and gently rest the crown of your head on the floor (do not put weight on it).
Open your chest fully. The weight should be on your forearms, not your head or neck.
Hold for 5 to 8 breaths. Breathe deeply into your chest.
To exit, lift your head, lower your back, and rest flat on the floor.
Opens the chest and throat
Stretches the front of the neck and shoulders
Counter pose to shoulder stand and forward folds
Improves posture and breathing capacity
Energizing and uplifting
No equipment needed

description.en: The garland pose malasana is a deep squat hip opener performed in a wide deep squat. The hands come together at the chest and the elbows press against the inside of the knees to open the hips wider. The pose stretches the adductors, calves, and ankles.

en: Stand with feet slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Point the toes slightly out.
Squat down as deep as possible with feet flat.
Bring your hands together in front of your chest in a prayer position.
Press the elbows against the inside of your knees.
Use the elbows to push the knees wider apart.
Sit tall in the deep squat with the chest up.
Hold the pose and breathe deeply then come back up.
Deep hip opener
Stretches the adductors
Mobilizes the ankles
Useful for squat depth
No equipment needed
Strong yoga pose

description.en: The hanging deadbug is an advanced core exercise that combines a dead hang with deadbug-style contralateral arm and leg movements. While hanging from a bar with one arm, the other arm and the opposite leg move in coordinated patterns. The exercise demands extreme core control and grip strength.

en: Hang from a pull up bar with both hands shoulder-width apart.
Bring your knees up to 90 degrees in a tucked hang position.
Brace your core hard.
Release one hand from the bar and reach forward.
At the same time, extend the opposite leg straight out.
Hold the contralateral position briefly.
Return the hand to the bar and tuck the leg back to start.
Switch sides on the next rep.
Advanced core stability work
Builds anti-rotation core strength
Challenges grip strength
Strong lat engagement to hang
Develops total body control
Useful for advanced ab training

description.en: The hip external rotator stretch targets the deep external rotators of the hip — the piriformis, gemelli, obturators, and quadratus femoris. Performed seated or supine with the leg crossed in figure-four position, it relieves outer hip and sciatic tension.

en: Sit on a chair or the floor with feet flat. Cross your right ankle over your left knee, just above the kneecap.
Flex your right foot to protect the knee.
Sit up tall. Place your right hand gently on your right knee.
Lean forward from the hips with a flat back until you feel a deep stretch in your right outer hip and glute.
Optionally, gently press your right knee down with your hand to deepen the stretch.
Hold for 30 to 60 seconds. Breathe deeply and relax into the stretch.
Switch sides and repeat.
The stretch should be felt in the glute, not the knee. If you feel knee pain, ease back.
Targets the deep hip external rotators
Relieves outer hip and sciatic tension
Improves hip mobility for squats and lateral movements
Practical for office or daily use
No equipment needed
Calming and restorative

description.en: The jump box over is a plyometric drill where the lifter jumps laterally over a box. From a side stance the athlete jumps up onto the box and continues down the other side in one motion. The drill builds explosive power and conditioning.

en: Stand to the side of a sturdy box.
Set the feet shoulder-width apart.
Bend the knees and load the hips.
Swing the arms back and explode up and over the box.
Land softly on top of the box on both feet.
Continue down the other side with a soft landing.
Reset and jump back over to the starting side.
Continue jumping over the box back and forth.
Builds explosive power
Strong conditioning move
Trains lateral plyometrics
Useful for athletes
Trains lower body power
Strong cardio builder

description.en: The kettlebell alternating row holds two KBs in a bent-over position and rows them one at a time in alternating fashion. The alternating pattern keeps constant tension on the back while allowing each side brief recovery. It builds back endurance and core stability.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart holding a KB in each hand.
Hinge at the hips until torso is roughly 45 degrees to the floor. Back flat.
Let both KBs hang with arms extended.
Row the right KB up while keeping the left hanging.
Lower the right, then row the left.
Continue alternating in a smooth rhythm.
Maintain the hinge position throughout.
Aim for 10 to 12 reps per side.
Continuous back tension through alternating pattern
Extended time under tension
Builds back endurance
Core anti-rotation from unilateral pulling
Easy to set up
Engaging rowing variation

description.en: The kettlebell split snatch is a snatch variation where you catch the KB overhead in a split stance (one foot forward, one back) rather than in a bilateral stance. The split catch develops different hip and leg loading patterns and is used in some kettlebell sport events.

en: Stand with a KB between your feet. Grip with one hand.
Swing the KB back and drive your hips forward explosively (same as standard snatch).
As the KB rises, split your feet into a lunge stance — one foot forward, one back.
Catch the KB overhead with arm locked out in the split position.
Stand up by stepping your feet back together with the KB still overhead.
Lower the KB back to the swing position.
Continue for desired reps, then switch arms.
Master the standard KB snatch first.
Develops split-catch mechanics
Different hip and leg loading than standard snatch
Builds explosive overhead power
Trains timing and coordination
Carries over to Olympic lifting split catch
Full-body power exercise

description.en: The kneeling leg half circle is a hip mobility drill done on all fours. The mover lifts one leg and sweeps it in a half circle pattern from front to back. It is a useful warm-up drill for hip mobility.

en: Set up on hands and knees in a quadruped position.
Place the hands under the shoulders and knees under the hips.
Brace your core and keep the back flat.
Lift one leg straight back behind you.
Sweep the leg in a half circle out to the side.
Continue the sweep to the front of the body.
Reverse the path back to the start.
Finish all reps then switch sides.
Mobilizes the hips
Strong warm-up drill
Useful before training
Builds hip range
Activates the glutes

description.en: The lateral raise with towel is an old-school self-resistance move where a towel is held taut between the hands and the lifter pulls outward while raising the arms out to the sides. The constant tension on the towel turns a basic lateral raise into a serious side delt builder with no hardware.

en: Stand tall holding a towel taut between both hands at hip level.
Set your feet at shoulder-width and brace your core.
Pull outward on the towel to create tension.
Maintain that pull throughout the entire set.
Raise your arms out to the sides while keeping the towel taut.
Lift until your arms reach shoulder height.
Pause briefly and squeeze the side delts.
Lower the arms back to the start while maintaining tension.
Builds side delt detail
No hardware needed
Constant tension method
Travel-friendly
Old-school technique
Useful at-home move

description.en: The lever leg extension is a single-joint isolation exercise performed on a dedicated leg extension machine. Sitting with the shins behind a padded roller, you extend your knees to lift the weight straight up by contracting only the quadriceps. It is the most direct quadriceps isolation exercise available and the gold standard for adding quad detail and size after compound work.

en: Sit on the leg extension machine and adjust the seat back so the back of your knees rests against the edge of the seat pad.
Adjust the ankle pad so it sits comfortably across your shins, just above your feet.
Grip the handles or sides of the seat firmly. Sit upright with your back pressed against the pad.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Extend both knees by lifting the pad up. Keep your hips planted on the seat — do not lift them.
Continue extending until your legs are fully straight (or nearly so). Squeeze your quads hard for one second at the top.
Lower the pad under control over a count of two to three seconds back to the starting position.
Stop just before the weight stack touches down to maintain tension on the quads.
The most direct isolation exercise for the quadriceps
Constant tension throughout the entire range of motion
Allows safe, comfortable training to muscular failure
Useful for finishing the quads after compound leg work
Easy to load progressively in small increments
Trains the rectus femoris (hip flexor + quad) effectively

musclesWorked: Quadriceps (rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, vastus intermedius)

description.en: The long arm crunch performs a standard crunch with arms extended straight overhead (behind the head). The extended arms create a longer lever, making the crunch harder than hands-behind-head or hands-on-chest variations.

en: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat.
Extend both arms straight overhead behind your head, biceps by your ears.
Keep your arms straight and in this position throughout.
Crunch up by lifting your shoulders off the floor.
Your extended arms rise with your torso — they do not swing forward.
Squeeze your abs at the top.
Lower under control.
Aim for 12 to 20 reps per set.
Longer lever arm increases ab demand
Harder than standard crunches without added weight
No equipment needed
Simple progression from standard crunches
Builds ab strength effectively
Easy to learn

description.en: The lever standing hip extension is a glute isolation exercise on a dedicated machine where you stand on one leg and press the other leg backward against a padded lever. The guided motion isolates the gluteus maximus through hip extension without lower-back involvement.

en: Stand on the platform of the hip extension machine with your left foot. Position your right leg against the padded lever behind you.
Grip the handles for stability. Stand tall with core braced.
Press your right leg back and up against the lever by extending at the hip. Keep your torso upright.
Continue extending until your right thigh is behind your body. Squeeze your right glute hard.
Slowly let the lever return under control. Do not let the weight stack slam.
Complete all reps on the right side, then switch.
Keep the movement slow and controlled — momentum reduces glute activation.
Use moderate weight and higher reps (12 to 20).
Direct glute isolation with guided motion
No lower-back involvement
Trains one side at a time, exposing imbalances
Easy to load progressively
Excellent finisher for glute workouts
Useful for rehabilitation and glute activation

description.en: The medicine ball chest pass is an explosive upper-body power exercise where you stand facing a wall, hold a medicine ball at your chest, and explosively throw it into the wall. You catch the rebound and immediately throw again. It develops pressing power and reactive force generation.

en: Stand about 3 to 4 feet from a sturdy wall. Hold a medicine ball at your chest.
Stand in a staggered stance for stability.
Explosively push the ball forward into the wall from your chest — like a chest pass in basketball.
Use your chest, shoulders, and triceps to generate maximum force.
Catch the rebound. Absorb the catch by letting the ball return to your chest.
Immediately throw again — minimize the time between catch and throw.
Continue for the desired reps. Use maximum effort each rep.
Aim for 10 to 15 throws per set.
Develops explosive pressing power
Builds reactive force generation
No deceleration phase — maximum velocity
Solo-friendly (wall catch)
Carries over to bench press and pushing sports
Time-efficient power exercise

description.en: The medicine ball step behind rotational throw uses a step behind footwork pattern to load the hips before rotating and slamming the ball into a wall. The motion builds rotational power for athletic performance.

en: Stand sideways to a sturdy wall holding a medicine ball at chest height.
Set up a few feet from the wall.
Step the back foot behind the front foot to load the back hip.
Brace the core and rotate the torso away from the wall.
Drive the back hip and shoulder forward toward the wall.
Release the ball and throw it into the wall with force.
Catch the ball off the rebound or pick it back up.
Reset and repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Builds rotational power through the hips and core.
Step behind footwork loads the back hip.
Trains athletic rotation for sport.
Improves total body coordination.
Carryover to throwing and swinging sports.
Develops oblique and core strength.

description.en: The PVC hip hinge is a movement teaching drill where you hold a PVC pipe or broomstick along your spine (touching head, upper back, and tailbone) while performing a hip hinge. The pipe provides instant feedback — if any of the three contact points lifts off, your spine is rounding. It is the gold standard drill for teaching the deadlift and RDL pattern.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hold a PVC pipe or broomstick vertically behind you.
The pipe should touch three points: the back of your head, your upper back (thoracic spine), and your tailbone.
Hold the pipe with one hand behind your neck and one hand at your lower back.
Push your hips straight back while keeping all three contact points on the pipe.
Bend your knees slightly. Keep your back completely flat.
Continue hinging until you feel a stretch in your hamstrings.
Drive your hips forward to stand back up, maintaining all three contact points.
Repeat 10 to 15 times as a pattern drill before deadlifting.
Gold standard drill for teaching hip hinge mechanics
Instant feedback on spinal position
Develops proper deadlift and RDL pattern
No weight needed — pure movement learning
Excellent warm-up before hinge exercises
Prevents lower-back rounding under load

description.en: The resistance band adduction split squat is a split squat with a resistance band anchored to the side, pulling the front leg outward. To maintain the split stance against the band tension, the adductors and glutes have to fire harder than usual. The drill builds inner thigh strength alongside the squat.

en: Anchor a resistance band at ankle height to your side.
Loop the band around your front (right) thigh just above the knee.
Step the right leg forward into a split stance.
Position the left leg behind in lunge position.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Lower into a split squat by bending both knees.
Resist the band pulling your right knee outward by activating the adductors.
Drive up through the front foot to standing. Switch sides after the set.
Strong adductor engagement
Builds inner thigh strength
Trains knee tracking
Different stimulus than standard split squat
Useful for hip stability work
Adds variety to leg training

description.en: Resistance band hip thrusts are a glute-building exercise where a band is looped across the hip crease and anchored under the feet during hip thrusts. This is essentially the same as the resistance band hip thrust — maximum band tension occurs at the top where glute activation peaks.

en: Sit on the floor with upper back against a bench. Loop a resistance band across your hip crease and anchor both ends under your feet.
Bend your knees at 90 degrees. Feet flat, hip-width apart.
Drive through your heels to thrust your hips up.
At the top, your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Squeeze your glutes hard.
The band tension is highest here — at peak glute contraction.
Lower under control.
Repeat for 12 to 20 reps.
Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Progressive glute loading at home
Maximum tension at peak glute contraction
Highly portable
Excellent glute builder
Easy to scale by band thickness
Useful when no barbell is available

description.en: The resistance band side step with horizontal pallof hold is a hybrid drill that combines lateral steps with a Pallof press. The setup uses two bands to load the hips and core simultaneously while training anti-rotation strength.

en: Loop a band around both ankles for the lateral steps.
Anchor a second band at chest height to one side.
Hold the chest band with both hands extended out front.
Set the feet shoulder width with both bands tensioned.
Brace the core and resist the chest band rotation.
Step laterally away from the chest band anchor.
Bring the trail foot in to maintain the wide stance.
Continue for the working set then switch sides.
Trains hip abduction.
Builds anti-rotation core.
Hits the glute medius.
Useful for athletes.
Improves hip stability.

description.en: The resistance band standing down warming up is a light activation drill. Pulling a band straight down against the body warms up the lats and triceps and primes them for pulling work.

en: Anchor a resistance band overhead.
Stand under the anchor and grab the band with both hands.
Hold the band straight overhead.
Brace the core and keep the chest up.
Pull the hands straight down past the hips.
Squeeze the lats hard at the bottom.
Pause briefly at full extension.
Return to the start and continue for the working set.
Warms up the lats.
Activates the triceps.
Useful pre-workout.
Improves shoulder health.
Builds the upper back.

description.en: The reverse crunch kick performs a reverse crunch (curling hips up) and adds a leg extension (kick) at the top before lowering. The kick adds extra hip flexor and lower ab demand beyond a standard reverse crunch.

en: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet off the floor. Hands at sides or under hips.
Curl your hips up by pulling your knees toward your chest (reverse crunch).
At the top, extend (kick) both legs straight up toward the ceiling.
Bend your knees back and lower your hips to the floor.
That is one rep.
The kick at the top adds extra demand.
Move with control throughout.
Aim for 10 to 15 reps.
Adds extra demand beyond standard reverse crunches
Targets lower abs and hip flexors
No equipment needed
Progressive from standard reverse crunches
Engaging variation
Builds lower ab control

description.en: The roll ball erector spinae is a self myofascial release drill for the long muscles that run along the spine. A small ball pressed into the erectors releases tightness from heavy lifting and prolonged sitting.

en: Lie on the back with the knees bent and feet flat.
Place a massage ball next to the spine in the lower back.
Brace the core and keep the head supported.
Lift the hips slightly to load the ball.
Roll the back slowly over the ball.
Pause on tender spots for several breaths.
Move the ball up the back along the erector line.
Continue for the working time then switch sides.
Releases the back muscles.
Improves spinal mobility.
Reduces lower back tightness.
Useful after heavy lifting.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The roll ball rectus abdominis is a self myofascial release drill for the abs. Pressing a ball into the rectus abdominis releases tightness that contributes to forward posture and shallow breathing.

en: Lie on the floor face down.
Place a massage ball under the abs.
Brace the upper body on the forearms.
Keep the body relaxed over the ball.
Take slow deep breaths into the belly.
Roll the abs slowly over the ball.
Pause on tender spots for several breaths.
Continue for the working time.
Releases the abs.
Improves trunk mobility.
Reduces front body tightness.
Useful for postural correction.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The roll ball scapula levator is a self myofascial release drill for the muscle connecting the neck to the shoulder blade. Pressing a ball into the levator scapulae releases tightness that contributes to neck pain and headaches.

en: Stand with the back to a wall.
Place a massage ball between the upper inner shoulder blade and the wall.
Brace the core and keep the body tall.
Press into the ball with controlled pressure.
Roll slowly across the levator area.
Pause on tender spots for several breaths.
Tip the head gently to find the muscle.
Continue for the working time then switch sides.
Releases the levator scapulae.
Reduces neck tightness.
Improves shoulder mobility.
Useful for desk workers.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The roll rhomboids uses a foam roller to release tension in the rhomboids and upper back muscles. Lying on your back with the roller positioned between the shoulder blades, you roll over the area to release tightness. The drill helps with desk-induced upper back tension and improves thoracic mobility.

en: Place a foam roller on the floor.
Lie on your back with the roller positioned between your shoulder blades.
Support your head with your hands behind it.
Bend your knees with feet flat on the floor.
Lift your hips slightly off the floor.
Brace your core and breathe slowly.
Slowly roll up and down through the upper back area.
Hold tender spots for 20 to 30 seconds.
Releases upper back tension
Improves thoracic mobility
Helps with desk-induced tightness
Recovery drill for upper body lifters
Improves posture
Easy to do at home

description.en: The roll triceps side lying on floor is a self myofascial release drill for the back of the upper arm. Lying on the side with a foam roller under the triceps releases tightness from heavy pressing and overhead work.

en: Lie on one side with a foam roller under the back of the upper arm.
Set the bottom arm extended overhead.
Stack the legs for balance.
Brace the body on the bottom forearm.
Keep the upper body relaxed over the roller.
Roll the triceps slowly along the roller.
Pause on tender spots for several breaths.
Cover the full upper arm then switch sides.
Releases the triceps.
Reduces upper arm tightness.
Improves elbow mobility.
Useful after pressing work.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The shuffle (lateral shuffle or side shuffle) is a lateral agility drill where you move sideways in an athletic stance with quick, sliding steps. It builds lateral quickness, hip stability, and cardiovascular conditioning. It is a foundational footwork drill used in basketball, tennis, football, and general athletic training.

en: Stand in an athletic stance — feet wider than shoulder-width, knees bent, hips back, chest tall.
Shift your weight to your right foot and push off, sliding your body to the left.
Step with your left foot, then slide your right foot to follow. Do not let your feet touch or cross.
Stay low in the athletic stance throughout. Keep your hips back and your center of gravity low.
Continue shuffling to the left for the desired distance (10 to 20 feet), then shuffle back to the right.
Pump your arms naturally for balance and speed.
Stay on the balls of your feet. Move quickly but under control.
Perform for time (20 to 45 seconds) or distance.
Builds lateral quickness and agility
Develops hip stability and ankle strength
Excellent cardiovascular conditioning
Foundational footwork drill for all court and field sports
No equipment needed
Trains the adductors and abductors dynamically

description.en: The single-leg bridge performs a glute bridge with one foot on the floor and the other leg extended or raised. Training one leg at a time doubles the glute demand per side and exposes left-right imbalances.

en: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat.
Extend your left leg straight up toward the ceiling (or straight forward).
Drive through your right heel to thrust your hips up.
Squeeze your right glute at the top. Body forms a line from right knee to shoulders.
Lower under control.
Complete reps, then switch legs.
Keep your hips level — do not let the unsupported side drop.
Aim for 12 to 15 reps per leg.
Doubles glute demand per leg
Exposes left-right imbalances
Builds single-leg hip extension strength
No equipment needed
Develops core anti-rotation
Progresses to weighted single-leg bridges

description.en: The Smith hex press is an inner-chest focused press variation where you press the bar on a Smith machine with hands held very close together (like the dumbbell hex press but with a bar). The narrow grip and active inner-squeeze pressure create constant inner-chest tension throughout the press.

en: Set up a flat bench under the Smith machine bar. Lie back on the bench with the bar over your chest.
Grip the bar with both hands very close together — about 6 inches apart, almost touching.
Unrack the bar by twisting it. Hold it above your chest with arms extended.
Brace your core. Press your hands actively toward each other against the bar.
Lower the bar slowly to your chest, maintaining the inner squeeze.
Press the bar back up to lockout, continuing to squeeze your hands together.
Squeeze your chest hard at the top.
Use moderate weight. Aim for higher reps focused on the squeeze.
Targets the inner chest specifically
Smith machine eliminates balance demand
Active inner-squeeze creates constant chest tension
Builds chest separation
Easier on the shoulders
Useful chest finisher

musclesWorked: Triceps brachii (heavy involvement from close grip)

description.en: The standing chest stretch against a door uses a doorway to lengthen the chest and front shoulder. With the forearm pressed into the door frame, stepping forward opens the chest.

en: Stand in an open doorway.
Bend one elbow at ninety degrees and place the forearm against the door frame.
Position the elbow at shoulder height.
Step the same side foot forward through the doorway.
Brace the core and keep the chest tall.
Allow the chest to open as the body moves forward.
Feel the stretch across the front of the chest and shoulder.
Hold the stretch for the desired duration then switch sides.
Opens the chest and front shoulders.
Reduces tension from desk work.
No equipment needed beyond a doorway.
Easy to perform at home.
Improves shoulder mobility.
Carryover to overhead lifts and bench press.

description.en: The standing iliotibial (IT) band stretch is a standing flexibility exercise where you cross one leg behind the other and reach the same-side arm overhead and across, deepening a side stretch. It targets the IT band — the long fascial band that runs along the outside of the thigh — and the lateral hip stabilizers.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Cross your right leg behind your left leg, planting your right foot on the floor outside your left foot.
Reach your right arm up and over to the left, like you are reaching across to your left side.
Push your right hip out to the right.
Feel the deep stretch along the entire right outside leg from hip to knee, plus the right side body.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply.
Switch legs and repeat on the other side.
Avoid bouncing — let gravity deepen the stretch.
Targets the IT band specifically
Stretches the lateral hip and obliques
Useful for runners and cyclists with tight IT bands
No equipment needed
Quick and accessible
Helps prevent IT band syndrome

description.en: The standing two side bend is a side bending mobility drill done with the arms reached overhead. The mover bends to one side then the other. It stretches the lats, obliques, and side trunk muscles.

en: Stand with the feet hip width apart.
Reach the arms straight overhead.
Clasp the hands together at the wrists.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Bend sideways to one side.
Feel the stretch along the side body.
Return to center then bend to the other side.
Continue alternating sides.
Stretches the obliques
Mobilizes the side body
Strong stretch drill
Useful warm-up
Builds spinal mobility

description.en: The static lunge kick combines a static lunge with a front kick. From the bottom of the lunge, you drive up and kick the front leg forward at hip height before stepping back into the next rep. The combination keeps the heart rate elevated while building leg and core strength.

en: Stand tall in a split stance with right foot forward.
Lower into a static lunge by bending both knees.
Continue down until your back knee almost touches the floor.
Drive up explosively through your front foot.
As you rise, kick the front leg forward at hip height.
Lower the kicking leg back to the starting position.
Repeat the lunge and kick on the same side for desired reps.
Switch sides and repeat.
Combines strength and cardio
Builds quad and glute strength
Strong core engagement to balance the kick
Improves balance and coordination
Time-efficient compound movement
No equipment required

description.en: The suspender leg curl, also known as the TRX hamstring curl, uses suspension straps anchored overhead. With your heels in the foot cradles and hips lifted in a bridge, you curl your heels toward your glutes against bodyweight resistance. It builds hamstring strength and core stability simultaneously.

en: Anchor suspension straps overhead with the foot cradles hanging at calf height.
Lie on your back beneath the straps with heels in the foot cradles.
Extend your arms by your sides for stability.
Drive through your heels to lift your hips into a glute bridge position.
Maintain the bridge with shoulders, hips, and knees in a straight line.
Curl your heels toward your glutes by bending the knees.
Pause at the top with knees bent and hips still elevated.
Slowly extend your legs back to the straight bridge position.
Builds hamstring strength without weights
Strong glute and core engagement
Bodyweight progression to heavier curls
Easy to scale by changing strap length
Useful for home or travel training
Develops single-leg control over time

description.en: The suspender single arm rear delt row is a unilateral TRX row done with the elbow flared wide. The wide elbow position biases the rear delts. It builds the rear delts and upper back one side at a time.

en: Set the suspension trainer at chest height.
Grip one handle with one hand.
Walk the feet forward until the body leans back.
Set the body in a straight line from head to heels.
Brace your core and keep the body straight.
Pull the handle to the chest with the elbow flared wide.
Squeeze the rear delt hard at the top.
Lower with control. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Targets the rear delts
Strong unilateral move
Trains each side
Builds upper back
Useful TRX move
Builds shoulder shape
